intro/hello: This lecture is about what comes after training: serving a model to people, fast and cheaply.
intro/forever: But it is served every time anyone uses it: every token of every answer is another forward pass.
intro/surprise: The surprise at its center: generating text is slow for a reason that has little to do with arithmetic.
intro/wait: Generating a token for one user, a GPU spends almost all its time waiting for memory.
intro/plan: Once you see that, the tricks follow: batching, paged attention, quantization, and speculative decoding.
intro/distill: We end with distillation, and with the tradeoff between latency and throughput.
intro/example: Our running example is Llama three, eight B, eight billion parameters, on one H one hundred GPU.
prefill/loop: A language model writes one token at a time: run the model, sample a token, append it, repeat.
prefill/cache: A server keeps the keys and values of earlier tokens in the K V cache, so each step computes only the newest token.
prefill/prefill: First, prefill. The whole prompt is known, so all its tokens go through the model in one pass.
prefill/ttft: Prefill fills the cache and gives the first new token. Its duration is the time to first token.
prefill/decode: Then, decode. Each new token depends on the last, so each needs a pass of its own, with one token in it.
prefill/tpot: Its duration, the time per output token, is how fast the answer streams onto the screen.
prefill/flops: How much arithmetic is a pass? Each weight does a multiply and an add per token: about two N operations for N parameters.
prefill/fast: For our model, sixteen billion per token. An H one hundred could do that in sixteen microseconds.
prefill/slow: In fact, a decode step takes about five milliseconds: three hundred times longer. Where does the time go?
roofline/two: An H one hundred has two speeds, and they are very different.
roofline/peak: Its compute: nearly a thousand trillion operations per second, on sixteen-bit numbers.
roofline/bw: Its memory bandwidth: three point three five trillion bytes per second.
roofline/ratio: Divide the two: the chip does about two hundred and ninety five operations in the time it takes to fetch one byte.
roofline/intensity: What matters is an operation's arithmetic intensity, I: operations per byte moved.
roofline/matmul: When a weight matrix multiplies B token vectors, each weight fetched is used once per token. The intensity is about B.
roofline/roof: The roofline model: the time is the larger of operations over peak, and bytes over bandwidth.
roofline/plot: On log axes, that is a rising slope, limited by memory, meeting a flat roof, limited by compute, at the ridge.
roofline/decode: A decode step for one user has B equal to one. It fetches every weight to use it exactly once.
roofline/slope: That puts it far down the slope, at one operation per byte. A long prefill sits past the ridge.
roofline/answer: Sixteen gigabytes at three point three five terabytes per second take four point eight milliseconds, with the arithmetic units over ninety nine percent idle.
batching/idea: If each fetch of the weights serves only one token, the cure is to make it serve many.
batching/batch: A server decodes the next token for B users in one step. Every weight matrix now multiplies B rows instead of one.
batching/once: The weights still cross the bus once per step, so the step costs about the same, and yields B tokens.
batching/one: At batch one, our model makes about two hundred tokens per second.
batching/many: At batch sixty four, about eight thousand seven hundred: forty two times more, for one and a half times the time.
batching/user: Each user's tokens slow only a little. Total throughput is what the operator pays for: this is the first lever.
batching/cache: One part does not batch: every sequence reads its own K V cache, and nobody else can reuse it.
batching/long: With eight thousand tokens of context, the caches outweigh the weights, throughput falls to two and a half thousand, and the batch no longer fits.
batching/gqa: That is why shrinking the cache, with grouped-query attention or eight-bit caches, matters so much.
continuous/real: Real requests arrive at random, wanting answers of very different lengths.
continuous/static: Static batching groups requests, and runs each group until its last member finishes.
continuous/idle: Every request that finishes early leaves its slot idle, while newcomers wait.
continuous/picture: Here are thirty requests in six slots. The red hatching is wasted time; the work takes a hundred and twenty six steps.
continuous/cont: Continuous batching decides the batch again at every single step.
continuous/leave: When a sequence finishes, it leaves.
continuous/join: And a waiting request takes its slot on the very next step, after its prefill.
continuous/result: The same thirty requests finish in sixty four steps, about half the time.
continuous/orca: This is iteration-level scheduling, from the Orca system in 2022, now standard in serving engines.
paged/grow: Batching wants many sequences in memory, but each one's cache grows every step, to a length nobody knows in advance.
paged/reserve: Early servers reserved one contiguous slab per request, big enough for its longest possible answer.
paged/waste: Most answers stop far short, so most of each slab sits empty: real systems used only twenty to forty percent of it.
paged/paged: Paged attention, the heart of the V L L M server, borrowed the operating system's fix: virtual memory.
paged/blocks: Split the cache into small blocks of sixteen tokens.
paged/ondemand: A sequence takes one more block, from anywhere in memory, only when its last block fills up.
paged/table: A block table records where each sequence's blocks live, and the attention kernel follows it.
paged/free: When a sequence finishes, its blocks go straight back to the pool.
paged/tail: The only waste is the unfilled tail of each sequence's last block.
paged/result: Here, three times as many sequences run at once, and three times as many finish. The paper reported two to four times the throughput.
quant/bytes: If decode time is bytes over bandwidth, the most direct speedup is fewer bytes.
quant/idea: Quantization stores each weight in eight bits, or four, instead of sixteen: half the bytes, or a quarter.
quant/grid: An integer format has evenly spaced values. So we choose a scale, s: what one integer step is worth.
quant/absmax: The simplest is absmax: the largest weight lands on the largest integer, a hundred and twenty seven in int eight, or seven at four bits.
quant/round: Then divide every weight by s, and round to the nearest whole number. That integer is what we store.
quant/back: To use it, multiply back by s. Each weight is now off by at most half a step.
quant/catch: The catch: one single large weight sets the step size for every other weight.
quant/relu: Absmax also wastes codes on lopsided values, like ray-loo outputs, which are never negative.
quant/zp: Zero-point quantization maps the actual range, from min to max, onto every code.
quant/z: And it stores one more number, the zero point z: the integer that stands for exactly zero.
quant/bits: Each extra bit halves the step and the error: about six decibels per bit.
outliers/share: How many weights should share one scale?
outliers/tensor: Per-tensor quantization uses one scale for a whole matrix. Cheap, but its largest weight sets the step everywhere.
outliers/crush: Here, at four bits, a row of small weights collapses onto just three values.
outliers/chan: Per-channel quantization gives every row its own scale, so small rows get a fine grid of their own.
outliers/group: At four bits, the norm is a scale per group of a few dozen weights, for a fraction of a bit extra.
outliers/acts: Activations are harder. From about seven billion parameters up, a few features carry values up to twenty times larger than the rest.
outliers/break: Quantize them together, and the scale they force on each token crushes the ordinary features.
outliers/int8: L L M int eight finds the few features that ever reach magnitude six, and multiplies just those in sixteen bits.
outliers/rest: Everything else runs in int eight: more than ninety nine point nine percent of the multiplications.
outliers/int4: At four bits, plain rounding loses too much. G P T Q corrects for each column's rounding as it goes, and A W Q protects the channels that meet the largest activations.
outliers/fp8: Newer GPUs also compute in eight-bit floats, F P eight, which shrinks activations too, and speeds up compute-bound work.
specidea/single: Batching serves more users. It does nothing for one user waiting on a long answer.
specidea/spec: Speculative decoding speeds up that one user, without changing the output distribution at all.
specidea/roof: It rests on the roofline: checking five tokens in one pass costs about as much as making one.
specidea/draft: So a small, fast draft model, with distribution q, guesses k tokens, one at a time. Each guess is cheap.
specidea/verify: Then the big target model, with distribution p, runs once on all k guesses together, like a tiny prefill.
specidea/positions: That one pass gives p at every guessed position, and at one more after them.
specidea/walk: Now walk left to right, keeping or rejecting each guess.
specidea/reject: At the first rejection, a corrected token is drawn, and the rest of the guesses are thrown away.
specidea/bonus: If all k survive, the target's distribution at the end gives a bonus token for free.
specidea/range: So every pass of the big model yields at least one token, and up to k plus one.
specrule/rule: Here is the rule. Keep the draft's token x with probability p of x over q of x, capped at one.
specrule/like: If the target likes the token at least as much as the draft did, always keep it.
specrule/over: If the draft was overconfident, keep it only part of the time, in proportion.
specrule/resid: On a rejection, sample from the residual: the part of p that sticks out above q, renormalized.
specrule/under: Rejections take probability away where q is too high; the residual puts it back where q is too low.
specrule/proof: Why exactly p? The draft proposes x and keeps it with probability q times p over q, capped: the smaller of p and q.
specrule/alpha: Add that up over all tokens, and you get alpha, the overall chance a guess is kept.
specrule/left: A rejection happens with probability one minus alpha, and the residual's total is also one minus alpha. They cancel.
specrule/sum: So the rejected path adds back exactly what the kept path is missing: the two add up to p, for every token, with no approximation.
specrule/check: You can check it by brute force: run thousands of passes, and the output frequencies settle onto p.
specspeed/one: Suppose each guess survives with probability alpha. A pass always yields one token.
specspeed/two: It yields a second if the first guess survives: probability alpha.
specspeed/three: A third if the first two survive: alpha squared. And so on, up to k plus one.
specspeed/sum: The expected count is a geometric series, with a short closed form.
specspeed/eg: With alpha at zero point eight and four guesses, that is about three point four tokens per pass, with a cap of five.
specspeed/cost: Guesses are not free. If a draft step costs c of a target step, a pass costs k times c, plus one.
specspeed/best: With a draft twenty times faster than the target, the best gain is about three times.
specspeed/fit: A draft that agrees with its target beats a fast one. The papers reported two to three times faster decoding, with identical outputs.
distill/change: Everything so far serves a fixed model more efficiently. The bluntest tool changes the model.
distill/student: Distillation trains a small student to imitate a big teacher, and serves the student.
distill/soft: The student learns to match the teacher's whole distribution, softened by a temperature, tau.
distill/why: That says far more than the one token that came next: which words were likely, and which absurd.
distill/kl: The loss is the K L divergence from teacher to student: zero when they agree on every token.
distill/llm: For language models, the teacher often just writes text for the student to learn from. That is how DeepSeek distilled R one into small models.
distill/tradeoff: Finally, the numbers a server is judged by pull against each other.
distill/ttft: Time to first token, set by waiting and by the prefill.
distill/tpot: Time per output token, set by the decode step.
distill/thr: And throughput: tokens per second per GPU, which sets the cost of every token.
distill/pick: Bigger batches raise throughput and slow each user. A server picks the point on this curve that still meets its latency target.
outro/mem: To sum up: decode is memory-bound, reading every weight to use it once.
outro/batch: Batching shares each weight read among many users.
outro/cont: Continuous batching refills a slot the moment it frees.
outro/paged: Paged attention stores caches in small blocks, so more sequences fit.
outro/quant: Quantization shrinks the bytes, with finer scales and care for outliers.
outro/spec: Speculative decoding drafts and verifies, and the accept rule keeps the output exactly p.
outro/distill: And distillation makes a smaller model to serve.
outro/next: The thread through all of it: a token costs bytes, not arithmetic. Every trick moves fewer bytes, or gets more from each one.
